This method computes surface normals for an isosurface mesh extracted via Marching Cubes by approximating the gradient of the underlying scalar field at the vertex positions using central differences, then normalizing the result [S1, unofficial][S3, unofficial].

The claim states that the method computes surface normals by approximating the gradient of the underlying scalar field at vertex positions using central differences, then normalizing the result. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this: it notes that the method 'Computes surface normals... by approximating the gradient of the underlying scalar field using central differences, then normalizing the result.' It provides the specific mathematical formulas for the central difference approximation and the normalization step ($n = -grad(f) / ||grad(f)||$). Source [S3] supports the general approach of calculating normals by sampling the scalar field (voxel data) at vertex positions, although it describes the implementation details slightly differently (using normalized coordinates to sample). Since the core mechanism described in the claim (gradient approximation via central differences on the scalar field) is explicitly detailed and supported by Source [S1], and Source [S3] aligns with the general concept of deriving normals from the scalar field at vertices, the evidence supports the claim.

The negative sign ensures the normal points in the direction of decreasing scalar value (outward for typical density fields), though this depends on the field's definition [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly provides the formula for the normal vector as $n = -frac{nabla f}{||nabla f||}$. The negative sign in this formula mathematically ensures that the normal vector points in the direction opposite to the gradient. Since the gradient points in the direction of the greatest rate of increase of the scalar field, the negative gradient points in the direction of decreasing scalar value. This aligns perfectly with the claim.
